catalog_quote: For tone placement in Malila, it is necessary to count morae. Short syllables are monomoraic and can carry only a single tone; long syllables are bimoraic and can bear two tones. Canonical noun and verb stems consist of two syllables: -CVCV, or -CVVCV; this means that they have two or three morae. ... Verb infinitives have no contrastive tonal melodies but they carry a High tone on the antepenultimate mora; see the examples of vowel length above in (4). This means that the H tone is sometimes realised on the root or stem, and sometimes on the class prefix. ... Nouns in their citation forms exhibit four contrastive tonal melodies. Each tone occupies one mora. 1. LLHL 2. LHLL 3. H ... L H L 4. H ... L L L ... L L H L: H tone on the penultimate mora ... L H L L: H tone on the antepenultimate mora ... H ... new_statements.translation: SIL 2018 passage: 'Malila is a tone language, that is, the pitch contours of words help to distinguish different meanings. ... With the meaning "they have cooked" the high pitch is on shi, i.e. we pronounce bhateleSHIle. With the meaning "they cooked (long ago)" the high pitch is on bha, i.e. we pronounce BHAteleshile.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls or mentions stress at all. Malila is described as a (restricted, mora-counting) tone language: in citation forms every H tone is located by counting morae from the end of the word -- verb infinitives carry a single predictable H on the antepenultimate mora; nouns carry one of four lexical melodies (H on penultimate mora; H on antepenultimate mora; H on augment/prefix plus H on penultimate mora; H on the first mora only); verbs additionally use H-tone position for TAM contrasts (SIL 2018, Mwashota 2016). Vowel length is contrastive and also compensatory, restricted to a four-mora window from the word end.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Three-mora nouns (classes 5, 9/10 with monomoraic roots) neutralise the four noun melodies to two; augment vowel lengthened to satisfy a four-mora minimum (Kutsch Lojenga 2007 §§3-6). No stress-related exceptions because no stress statement exists.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone in citation forms of nouns (augment+prefix+stem) and verb infinitives; SIL 2018 examples are inflected verbs in isolation. Nothing on phrase-level prominence or penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Malila [mgq] = Glottolog mali1279 (self-name Ishimalila/Shɨmalɨla; Swahili Kimalila), spoken around Ilembo, Mbeya Rural, SW Tanzania; no dialect differentiation is made (Kutsch Lojenga's data from consultant John Mbeyale; SIL materials from the Mbeya-based Malila team). Not to be confused with mali1284 or other 'Mali-' glottocodes.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Sec. 2.3 'Tone' (pp. 79-80): tone placement counts morae from the word end; verb infinitives have no contrastive melodies but carry H on the antepenultimate mora; nouns in citation form have four contrastive melodies (LLHL, LHLL, H.LHL, H.LLL), each tone on one mora; contrastive and compensatory vowel length; a four-mora minimality repair. The words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur.

sources.note: Nothing on stress (mkazo). Sec. 6 'Alama za mawimbi (toni)', printed p. 14 (PDF p. 18): 'Kimalila ni lugha ya toni' -- Malila is a tone language; position of the high pitch distinguishes e.g. bhateleSHIle 'they have cooked' from BHAteleshile 'they cooked (long ago)'; H-toned vowel is marked in writing on remote-past verbs. Sec. 3: contrastive vowel length written double (kʉpela 'drive' vs kʉpeela 'strain'). Swahili text is in a custom-encoded font; decoded copy.
